The photometry was performed using the RLMMS, an in-vehicle luminance system developed by the Virginia Tech Transportation Institute (VTTI). The RLMMS records data from four waterproof Minolta illuminance detector heads attached to a roof rack atop a vehicle. Each head is positioned on the end (facing upward) of each of four arms of the apparatus, which is also known as the “Spider.” Positioned in the center of the four arms is a NovaTel GPS device. A fifth Minolta detector is mounted to the forward windshield to detect oncoming glare. The RLMMS is coupled with luminance and color cameras that take snapshots of the roadway at a preset sampling rate. The cameras are connected to their own stand-alone computer that houses images; images can also be viewed on a single laptop screen along with the other data being collected in the vehicle using a Controller Area Network (CAN) reader. The cameras have been validated by rigorous calibration and tuning so that the camera can gather data for naturalistic driving research, and the equipment can be mounted to almost any vehicle. The layout of the RLMMS system is shown in Figure 22. This system is also capable of being mounted on a towed vehicle. 42 Figure 22. RLMMS (left); Spider assembly and GPS mounted atop an SUV (right). As these the measurements are coupled to GPS coordinates, mapping of the lighting levels on the roadway, along with the calculated lighting metrics is possible. A sample of this map is shown in Figure 23. 43 Figure 23. Sample GIS-based output of the measurement systems. Data collection was conducted September 19–23, 2020. The team traveled each roadway with the RLMMS system multiple times in order to measure lighting levels for all travel lanes. For roadways in Cambridge, the project team collected the lighting measurement data twice prior to 10:00 p.m. and after midnight. Within both cities, the final collected lighting data covered 46.6 miles of local roads and 64.6 miles of HPMS roadways. The following describes the methods used along with the rationale on why the methods were selected. 4.1.3.1 Negative Binomial Regression with Random Effects Negative binominal regression is a regression technique that is particularly suitable for overdispersed count data (i.e., the variance is greater than the mean). Due to this reason, negative binominal regression has been widely used for crash data analysis (Lord and Mannering, 2010; Donnel et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2019).
